out:
Northwind Logistics announced third-quarter earnings of $4.2 million for the period ending 30 September 2025, marking a year-over-year rise of eighteen percent. According to leadership, almost the entire improvement stemmed from the enterprise unit, which climbed thirty-four percent, while the consumer branch declined by about six percent. Marta Delacroix, serving as chief executive, called it the strongest performance since the company’s stock market debut in March 2021.

The enterprise gain was fueled by three agreements signed last month. The largest, inked with Bergstrom Manufacturing in July, runs for five years and is expected to deliver roughly $11.8 million across its term. Analyst projections had placed revenue within a band of $3.9 million to $4.1 million, so the actual figure exceeded the upper limit. Share price jumped seven percent after market close, then surrendered about half of those gains the next morning.

Costs rose but at a slower pace than income. Operating expenses climbed to $3.1 million in the quarter, an eleven percent increase from the prior year. Staffing accounted for most of that rise: Northwind counted 412 employees on 30 September, up from 361 one year earlier. Delacroix stated hiring would decelerate after September and finish the calendar year below 430 total employees.

The board approved a twelve-cent dividend per share, payable 14 November to shareholders recorded as of 31 October. This marks the fourth straight quarterly payout. The payout ratio now sits near twenty-two percent of net profit, and chief financial officer Peter Okonkwo said directors aim to keep it under thirty percent while continuing to fund logistics upgrades.

A one-time $480,000 expense was revealed for the winding down of a Rotterdam warehouse that shuttered 30 June. Northwind estimates the closure will shave roughly $1.3 million annually from fixed costs starting in 2026, with forty-seven workers either moved internally or offered exit packages. Okonkwo confirmed the charge is fully booked in Q3 results and no further costs are anticipated.

For the full twelve months of 2025, the business now expects revenue between $16.5 million and $17.2 million, translating to growth of fourteen to nineteen percent versus 2024. That outlook assumes no major slip in shipping rates, which fell nine percent industry-wide during the quarter per the Baltic Dry Index. Delacroix warned that consumer demand typically softens in the final three months and there is no expectation of recovery before mid-2026.

Post-results, several equity research houses adjusted their price targets. Kestrel Research lifted its mark from $18 to $21 but kept a hold suggestion, citing firmer margins but still-weak consumer demand. Harbourline Capital took a more bullish stance, changing its stance to buy with a $24 estimate, arguing the market was underappreciating the enterprise opportunity. Two other firms chose to leave their ratings unchanged.

Northwind will hold its yearly investor event in Chicago on 3 December, where executives plan to present a three-year roadmap targeting $25 million in yearly revenue by 2028. Delacroix has noted this goal will likely require at least two takeovers, though the last deal—the purchase of Palermo Freight for $2.4 million—closed in August 2023.
